variants.title: Run the supervised lifecycle
variants.context: Training is an experiment, not the finish line. The lesson runs the work as define the decision, build protected evidence, fit and compare against a baseline, then release with limits.
variants.prompt: A team is starting an ETA model that will be shown at checkout. Put the stages in order.

items.text: Build training, validation, and test boundaries that keep the same entity, future event, or duplicate out of two splits.
Fit candidates on training data, make feature and threshold choices on validation data, and compare every candidate with a simple baseline.
Evaluate slices, latency, and failures, then run shadow or canary traffic before the estimate controls the checkout page.
Name the prediction unit, target, prediction time, product action, and the mistakes the business cannot accept.

variants.hint: What has to be written down before any evidence is worth collecting?
variants.explanation: Frame, split, fit, operate. Each stage constrains the next, and a boundary drawn after training cannot protect the estimate.

variants.title: Run the supervised lifecycle
variants.context: Training is an experiment, not the finish line. The lesson runs the work as define the decision, build protected evidence, fit and compare against a baseline, then release with limits.
variants.prompt: A fraud team is replacing a rules engine with a learned model. Put the stages in order.

items.text: Train candidates and compare each of them with the existing rules engine on the validation set.
Assign every record of an account to one split so the same account cannot sit in both training and test.
Write down that the unit is one authorization, that the label is a confirmed chargeback, and that a missed fraud costs far more than a needless review.
Check error by issuing bank and device, then shadow the model before it is allowed to decline a payment.

variants.hint: The cost of each mistake is an input to the design, not an output of it.
variants.explanation: Naming the cost of mistakes first is what decides the split unit, the comparison baseline, and the release limits later.

variants.title: Run the supervised lifecycle
variants.context: Training is an experiment, not the finish line. The lesson runs the work as define the decision, build protected evidence, fit and compare against a baseline, then release with limits.
variants.prompt: A retailer wants weekly demand forecasts per item. Put the stages in order.

items.text: Report error for slow movers and promotion weeks, then run the forecast beside the planner before it drives ordering.
State that the store predicts next week units per item and that overstock and stockout cost different amounts.
Split by time so every validation and test week falls after the training weeks.
Fit candidates, choose the stopping point on validation weeks, and compare with a last year same week baseline.

variants.hint: Forecasting constrains one of these stages more than the others.
variants.explanation: The same four stages hold for forecasting, except the protected boundary must respect temporal order rather than only entity identity.

variants.title: Name the prediction contract
variants.context: A complete prediction contract names the prediction unit, the target and how its label is observed, the moment the prediction is needed, the features available at that moment, and the product action with the cost of mistakes.
variants.prompt: A delivery product must show an arrival estimate. Put the five contract items in the order the lesson defines them.

items.text: State the action and the cost: the shown promise sets expectation, and a late promise costs more than an early one.
State the prediction unit: one customer order.
State the target: minutes from checkout until the courier closes the trip, observed at delivery.
State the moment: the estimate is needed while the customer is still on the checkout page.
List the features that already exist at that moment, such as store, distance, hour, and current courier supply.

variants.hint: One item decides which evidence is admissible, so find where it has to sit.
variants.explanation: Unit, target, moment, available features, action and cost. Naming the moment before the features is what keeps a field created after the decision out of the model.

variants.title: Name the prediction contract
variants.context: A complete prediction contract names the prediction unit, the target and how its label is observed, the moment the prediction is needed, the features available at that moment, and the product action with the cost of mistakes.
variants.prompt: A payments team is framing a fraud score. Put the five contract items in order.

items.text: State the target: whether that attempt later becomes a confirmed chargeback, observed weeks afterwards.
State the unit: one card authorization attempt.
State the moment: the score is needed inside the authorization window, before the payment is approved.
List the evidence present at that instant, such as amount, merchant, device history, and velocity counters.
State the action: approve, decline, or review, where a wrong decline loses a customer and a wrong approval loses the money.

variants.hint: A label that arrives weeks later still belongs early in the contract.
variants.explanation: Label delay does not move the target down the list; it is described with the target so the team knows how long evidence takes to close.

variants.title: Name the prediction contract
variants.context: A complete prediction contract names the prediction unit, the target and how its label is observed, the moment the prediction is needed, the features available at that moment, and the product action with the cost of mistakes.
variants.prompt: A support tool will route new tickets to a team. Put the five contract items in order.

items.text: List the evidence available then: subject text, product area, plan, and account history.
State the moment: the routing decision happens the second the ticket is submitted.
State the target: the team that eventually resolves the ticket, recorded at closure.
State the unit: one newly created support ticket.
State the action: place the ticket in a queue, where a wrong route costs a reassignment and a slower first reply.

variants.hint: Resolution notes exist eventually, but the contract decides when they can be read.
variants.explanation: Writing the moment before the feature list is what stops resolution notes, written after the routing decision, from becoming an input.

variants.title: Compute the measure the decision needs
variants.context: Precision is how often positive predictions are right, recall is how many actual positives are found, and a calibrated probability of 0.8 should occur about 80 percent of the time for comparable cases.
variants.prompt: A fraud model flags 400 transactions during one week. 120 of the flagged transactions are confirmed fraud, and the week contained 300 confirmed fraud transactions in total. What is the recall of the model that week, in percent?
variants.hint: Recall asks about the positives that exist, not about the alerts that were raised.
variants.explanation: Recall is found positives divided by actual positives, so 120 of 300 is 40 percent. 120 of 400 would be precision instead.

mistakes.feedback: That is 120 divided by 400, which is precision.
That divides actual fraud by the flag count, which measures neither precision nor recall.

variants.title: Compute the measure the decision needs
variants.context: Precision is how often positive predictions are right, recall is how many actual positives are found, and a calibrated probability of 0.8 should occur about 80 percent of the time for comparable cases.
variants.prompt: A moderation queue receives 250 items flagged by the model in one day. Reviewers confirm 90 of them as violations, and the day actually contained 300 violations. What is the precision of the flags, in percent?
variants.hint: Precision looks only at the cases the model claimed were positive.
variants.explanation: Precision is confirmed positives divided by predicted positives, so 90 of 250 is 36 percent.

mistakes.feedback: That is 90 divided by 300, which is recall.
That is the share of flags that were wrong, which is one minus precision.

variants.title: Compute the measure the decision needs
variants.context: Precision is how often positive predictions are right, recall is how many actual positives are found, and a calibrated probability of 0.8 should occur about 80 percent of the time for comparable cases.
variants.prompt: A churn model assigns a predicted probability near 0.8 to 900 accounts this month. If the model is well calibrated in that bucket, about how many of those accounts should actually churn?
variants.hint: A calibrated probability is a rate you can apply to the whole bucket.
variants.explanation: Calibration means a predicted 0.8 matches roughly 80 percent of comparable cases, so about 720 of the 900 accounts should churn.

mistakes.feedback: That counts the accounts expected not to churn.
That reads 0.8 as a count out of 100 rather than a rate applied to 900 accounts.

variants.title: Diagnose the generalization gap
variants.context: Compare training quality with representative unseen quality. Both weak means underfitting, strong training with weak unseen quality means overfitting, and a deployment population that moved away from the evaluation evidence means distribution shift.
variants.prompt: A pricing model scores 0.61 on training data and 0.60 on a representative holdout, and both numbers sit below the simple baseline the team must beat. What does this pattern indicate?
options: Overfitting, so add regularization and stop the training run earlier.
Distribution shift, so rebuild the holdout from newer production traffic.
Underfitting, so improve signal, features, optimization, or capacity one step at a time.
optionFeedback: Wrong. Overfitting shows strong training quality beside weaker unseen quality, which is not this pattern.
Wrong. Shift separates production from the evaluation evidence, but here the training fit itself is weak.
Correct. Training and unseen quality are both weak, which means no useful fit has been learned yet.
variants.hint: Look at the absolute quality of both numbers, not only at the gap between them.
variants.explanation: When both numbers are weak the model has not learned enough, so add signal or capacity rather than restricting it further.

variants.title: Diagnose the generalization gap
variants.context: Compare training quality with representative unseen quality. Both weak means underfitting, strong training with weak unseen quality means overfitting, and a deployment population that moved away from the evaluation evidence means distribution shift.
variants.prompt: A delivery model reaches 2 minutes of mean absolute error on training orders and 11 minutes on a holdout drawn from the same weeks and the same cities. What does the gap indicate?
options: Underfitting, so raise capacity and add richer features to close the error.
Overfitting, so reduce capacity, regularize, stop earlier, or gather more representative data.
Distribution shift, so refresh the evaluation evidence from the newest traffic.
optionFeedback: Wrong. Training error of 2 minutes shows the model fit the training data well, so capacity is not the shortage.
Correct. Strong training quality with much weaker unseen quality is the signature of a fit that does not transfer.
Wrong. The holdout covers the same weeks and cities, so the population did not move.
variants.hint: Ask whether the fit failed or whether it failed to transfer.
variants.explanation: Overfitting is treated by reducing memorization or improving the evidence, not by adding capacity that widens the gap.

variants.title: Diagnose the generalization gap
variants.context: Compare training quality with representative unseen quality. Both weak means underfitting, strong training with weak unseen quality means overfitting, and a deployment population that moved away from the evaluation evidence means distribution shift.
variants.prompt: A demand model holds steady holdout error on last quarter's data, but since launch its error in one newly opened region is three times the aggregate. What does this indicate?
options: Underfitting, so add capacity because the model cannot represent the new region.
Distribution shift, so report that region as a slice and refresh the data boundary.
Overfitting, so shrink capacity until holdout and production agree again.
optionFeedback: Wrong. Underfitting would show weak quality everywhere, including on the holdout.
Correct. The deployment population now includes cases the evaluation evidence never covered.
Wrong. The holdout error did not degrade, so the training fit is not the thing that failed here.
variants.hint: Which explanation is about the population rather than about the fit?
variants.explanation: One aggregate score hides a moved population, so slice reporting and a refreshed data boundary come before retuning capacity.

variants.title: Keep the evaluation roles separate
variants.context: Training data changes parameters, validation data supports choices such as features, model family, thresholds, and stopping point, the test set gives a final estimate after those choices are frozen, and production slices reveal what one aggregate score hides.
variants.prompt: A team is writing down what each body of evidence is allowed to do. Match each one to its role.

pairs.label: Training set
pairs.detail: Changes the model parameters during fitting.

pairs.label: Validation set
pairs.detail: Supports choices such as features, model family, thresholds, and stopping point.

pairs.label: Test set
pairs.detail: Gives a final estimate once those choices are frozen.

pairs.label: Production slices
pairs.detail: Reveal populations, time periods, or conditions that one aggregate score hides.

variants.hint: Ask which decision each body of evidence is allowed to influence.
variants.explanation: Roles stay separate because evidence that influenced a choice can no longer give an unbiased estimate of that choice.

variants.title: Keep the evaluation roles separate
variants.context: Training data changes parameters, validation data supports choices such as features, model family, thresholds, and stopping point, the test set gives a final estimate after those choices are frozen, and production slices reveal what one aggregate score hides.
variants.prompt: Four tasks sit on the sprint board for a fraud model. Match each task to the evidence it belongs to.

pairs.label: Update the weights for each candidate model
Pick the score cutoff that fits the review capacity
Report the launch estimate after the design is frozen
Track error per issuing bank in the weeks after release

variants.hint: Every choice made with a body of evidence spends its ability to estimate.
variants.explanation: Parameters belong to training, choices to validation, the frozen estimate to the test set, and post launch inspection to slices.

variants.title: Keep the evaluation roles separate
variants.context: Training data changes parameters, validation data supports choices such as features, model family, thresholds, and stopping point, the test set gives a final estimate after those choices are frozen, and production slices reveal what one aggregate score hides.
variants.prompt: Match each question a reviewer asks to the evidence that can answer it honestly.

pairs.label: Did the optimization fit anything at all?
Which of two thresholds should ship?
How well will this do on cases nobody selected against?
Which group is being served worst right now?

variants.hint: Evidence already used to make a choice cannot also judge that choice.
variants.explanation: Repeatedly choosing a model on test results turns the test set into another validation set, so keep one genuinely untouched boundary.
